Molecular cloning. It's the process of isolating a DNA fragment of interest, inserting it into a vector, typically a plasmid, and introducing the recombinant molecule into host cells for propagation or expression. It is the foundational technique for creating transgenic organisms, producing recombinant proteins, and constructing genetic libraries. Plasmids are small, circular DNA molecules usually derived from bacteria that replicate independently in cells. They carry an origin of replication, selectable markers like antibiotic resistance, and cloning sites. The target DNA and vector are both cut with restriction enzymes at compatible sites, generating sticky ends—single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other. The DNA ligase enzyme seals the phosphodiester backbone between the insert and vector, creating a circular recombinant plasmid. Competent cells, whether bacteria or yeast, are made permeable and exposed to the recombinant plasmid. A small percentage take it up and incorporate it into their chromosome or maintain it on its own. Transformed colonies are identified by selectable markers, and the correct insert is confirmed by PCR, restriction digest, or sequencing. This classic method has been used since the nineteen seventies. Modern alternatives like Gibson assembly and TALEN slash CRISPR offer seamless, scarless insertion. Molecular cloning connects to DNA as the genetic material being cloned and manipulated, plasmids as the most common cloning vectors—cheap, well-characterized, and easy to propagate—restriction enzymes as the tools that cut DNA at specific sites to generate compatible ends, DNA ligase as the enzyme that rejoins DNA strands after restriction cutting, PCR which is often used to amplify the insert before cloning, and transformation as the method for introducing the recombinant plasmid into cells.
